questions.q: How will you distinguish between $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and $(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NH}$ by the Hinsberg test?
questions.solution:
The Hinsberg test treats the amine with **benzenesulphonyl chloride** ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}$, Hinsberg's reagent) and then with aqueous KOH. The two amines behave differently at the second stage.

**Ethylamine (primary, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$).**

It has **two** hydrogens on nitrogen. One is replaced by the sulphonyl group :

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{N}\text{C}_2\text{H}_5 \longrightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{NH}\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$$

The product still has an **N–H** hydrogen, and it is acidic because the strongly electron-withdrawing $-\text{SO}_2-$ group stabilises the resulting anion. So the product **dissolves in alkali**, giving a clear solution.

**Diethylamine (secondary, $(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NH}$).**

It has only **one** hydrogen on nitrogen, and that one is replaced :

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl} + \text{HN}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2 \longrightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{N}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2$$

The product has **no N–H** left, so it is not acidic and is **insoluble in alkali** — it stays as a solid or an oily layer.

**The distinction, in one line.**

**Amine · Product with KOH(aq)**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ · soluble — clear solution
$(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{NH}$ · insoluble — solid or oily layer

(A tertiary amine would not react with the reagent at all, having no N–H to replace.)

questions.q: In aqueous solution, the order of basicity among methylamines is:
questions.solution:
Three effects pull in different directions: alkyl groups **release electrons** (helping), they **crowd** the nitrogen (hindering), and the protonated ion is **stabilised by hydration** through its N–H bonds (fewer N–H, less help).

The result in water is the famous irregular order: $\mathbf{2° > 1° > 3°}$.

In the **gas phase**, with no solvent, the order is the simple $3° > 2° > 1°$ — proof that solvation is what distorts it.

questions.q: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because:
questions.solution:
The lone pair on nitrogen overlaps with the ring's $\pi$ system and is **delocalised**, so it is much less available to accept a proton.

$\text{p}K_{b}$: aniline $9.4$, ammonia $4.75$ — aniline is thousands of times weaker.

The same delocalisation is why aniline activates the ring so strongly towards electrophilic substitution: what the nitrogen gives up, the ring gains.
options: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring
it has a larger molar mass

questions.q: The carbylamine reaction is a test for:
questions.solution:
A **primary** amine with chloroform and alcoholic KOH gives an isocyanide, recognised instantly by its extremely offensive smell:

$\text{RNH}_{2} + \text{CHCl}_{3} + 3\text{KOH} \to \text{RNC} + 3\text{KCl} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Secondary and tertiary amines give no reaction, so it is a clean test for primary amines only.

questions.q: Benzenediazonium chloride is prepared by treating aniline with:
questions.solution:
**Diazotisation:** nitrous acid, generated in situ from $\text{NaNO}_{2}$ and HCl, at **$273$–$278$ K**.

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2} + \text{NaNO}_{2} + 2\text{HCl} \to \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-} + \text{NaCl} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The low temperature is essential: above about $278$ K the salt decomposes to phenol and nitrogen.

questions.q: Hofmann's bromamide degradation converts an amide to an amine with:
questions.solution:
$\text{RCONH}_{2} + \text{Br}_{2} + 4\text{NaOH} \to \text{RNH}_{2} + \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} + 2\text{NaBr} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The carbonyl carbon leaves as carbonate, so the amine has **one carbon fewer** than the amide, and it is always **primary**.

That makes it a rare way of going **down** the homologous series.
options: the same number of carbon atoms

questions.q: How many isomeric amines are possible with the formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{9}\text{N}$?
questions.solution: Propan-1-amine, propan-2-amine (both primary), N-methylethanamine (secondary) and trimethylamine (tertiary) — $\mathbf{4}$.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of aniline, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}$, in g/mol. (C $= 12$, H $= 1$, N $= 14$.)
In how many of these is the nitrogen attached to exactly two carbon atoms: trimethylamine, diethylamine, aniline, N-methylaniline?
questions.solution:
**Diethylamine** ✓ and **N-methylaniline** ✓ — both secondary.

Trimethylamine has three, aniline one. So $\mathbf{2}$.

The class of an amine is decided by the number of carbons on the **nitrogen**, not by the carbon skeleton — unlike alcohols.

questions.q: How many amine products (excluding the quaternary salt) can form when excess ethyl bromide reacts with ammonia?
questions.solution:
Primary, secondary and tertiary ethylamines — $\mathbf{3}$ (and then the quaternary ammonium salt).

Every amine formed is itself a nucleophile, so the reaction keeps going. This is exactly why **ammonolysis is a poor preparation** and why a large excess of ammonia is used to favour the primary amine.

questions.q: Find the percentage of nitrogen by mass in methanamine, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{2}$ (molar mass $31$ g/mol; N $= 14$), correct to one decimal place.
Explain the relative basicity of aliphatic amines, ammonia and aromatic amines, with the factors involved.
questions.solution:
**Order:** aliphatic amines $>$ ammonia $\gg$ aromatic amines.

**Aliphatic amines vs ammonia.** Alkyl groups release electrons inductively, increasing the electron density on nitrogen and making the lone pair more available. They also stabilise the resulting ammonium ion.

**Among aliphatic amines** the order in water is irregular — $2° > 1° > 3°$ — because three effects compete:

1. **+I effect** — more alkyl groups, more basic.

2. **Steric hindrance** — more alkyl groups, harder for a proton to reach.

3. **Solvation** — the ammonium ion is stabilised by hydrogen bonding through its N–H bonds, and a tertiary amine's ion has only one.

**Aromatic amines.** The lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so it is far less available. Aniline's $\text{p}K_{b}$ is $9.4$ against ammonia's $4.75$.

Protonating aniline also **destroys** the delocalisation, which costs energy the reaction cannot easily pay.

**Substituted anilines:** electron-withdrawing groups ($-\text{NO}_{2}$) reduce basicity further; electron-releasing groups ($-\text{CH}_{3}$, $-\text{OCH}_{3}$) increase it.

questions.q: Describe the preparation of benzenediazonium chloride and four of its synthetic uses.
questions.solution:
**Preparation (diazotisation).** Aniline in cold dilute HCl, treated with sodium nitrite at $273$–$278$ K:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2} + \text{NaNO}_{2} + 2\text{HCl} \to \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-} + \text{NaCl} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The salt is unstable and is used in solution at once.

**Uses — the $\text{N}_{2}^{+}$ group is the best leaving group in organic chemistry**, because it leaves as nitrogen gas.

1. **Sandmeyer reaction** — $\text{CuCl}/\text{HCl}$, $\text{CuBr}/\text{HBr}$ or $\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}$ gives chloro-, bromo- or cyanobenzene.

2. **Gattermann reaction** — copper powder and the halogen acid, doing the same job more cheaply but in poorer yield.

3. **Replacement by other groups** — warm water gives phenol, KI gives iodobenzene (no catalyst needed), $\text{HBF}_{4}$ then heat gives fluorobenzene, and hypophosphorous acid gives **benzene itself**.

4. **Coupling reactions** — with phenol or aniline in mildly alkaline or acidic solution, giving intensely coloured **azo dyes**:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-} + \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} \to p\text{-hydroxyazobenzene}$

**Why this matters synthetically.** Chlorobenzene cannot be made from benzene with any control over position, but a nitro group can be placed exactly where you want it, reduced to the amine, diazotised and replaced. The diazonium salt is the hinge of aromatic synthesis.

questions.q: How would you distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary amines in the laboratory?
questions.solution:
**1. Hinsberg's test** — with benzenesulphonyl chloride:

• **Primary:** gives a sulphonamide with an N–H that is acidic, so the product **dissolves in alkali**.

• **Secondary:** gives a sulphonamide with no N–H — a precipitate **insoluble in alkali**.

• **Tertiary:** has no N–H at all and **does not react**.

One reagent, three different outcomes — which is why this is the standard test.

**2. Carbylamine test** — chloroform and alcoholic KOH. Only a **primary** amine gives the foul-smelling isocyanide.

**3. With nitrous acid at $273$ K:**

• **Primary aliphatic:** brisk **nitrogen gas** and an alcohol.

• **Primary aromatic:** a stable diazonium salt (which couples with phenol to give an orange dye).

• **Secondary:** a yellow oily **nitrosamine**.

• **Tertiary:** simply forms a salt.

For a written answer, always give the reagent, the observation and the conclusion.

questions.q: Explain why aniline cannot be nitrated directly, and how the difficulty is overcome.
questions.solution:
**Two problems.**

1. **Nitrating mixture is strongly acidic,** so the aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion. That $-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ group is strongly electron-**withdrawing** and **meta**-directing, so a substantial amount of the meta product is formed — the opposite of what the free amine would give.

2. **Nitric acid is an oxidising agent,** and aniline is easily oxidised, so the reaction is messy and the yield poor.

**The remedy — protect the amino group.** Acetylate it first:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2} + (\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO})_{2}\text{O} \to \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NHCOCH}_{3}$ (acetanilide)

The amide nitrogen's lone pair is partly drawn into the carbonyl, so the group is **less basic** (it will not be protonated) and **less activating** — but still **ortho/para** directing.

Nitrate, then **hydrolyse** the amide back with acid or alkali:

acetanilide $\xrightarrow{\text{HNO}_{3}/\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}}$ p-nitroacetanilide $\xrightarrow{\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}}$ p-nitroaniline

**Protection and deprotection** is a general strategy in synthesis: put a group out of harm's way, do the chemistry, and restore it.
